newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland may need to import grain if rains persist.
newsitem.headline: Poland may need to import grain if rains persist.

text.p: Poland may need to import grain if rains continue during the harvest and damage crop quality, a government-linked analyst from the Agriculture Economics Institute said.

Michal Kisiel on Monday reiterated earlier grain loss estimates of between 500,000 and 800,000 tonnes as a result of floods in southern Poland, which would reduce 1997 output to 23.6-24.7 million tonnes.
Domestic demand in 1997 was estimated at 26.2 million tonnes, with current reserves at four million tonnes, he said.
"We assume that grain losses may be 500,000 to 800,000 tonnes, which does not invalidate our most recent estimate of this year's output of 23.6-24.7 million tonnes," Kisiel said.
Weeks of rain at the start of July caused floods in southern Poland which inundated almost 5,000 sq km of the country, killing 52 people so far and forcing tens of thousands out of their homes.
The precise impact the floods on Poland's agriculture are not yet known, but the harvest has been delayed for two to three weeks.
"If it continues to rain...as the delayed harvest finally begins, we might see a fall in the quality of the crops and imports would be necessary," he said, declining to give any estimate of imports.
In 1996 Poland produced 24.7 million tonnes of grain.
Last week Agriculture Minister Jaroslaw Kalinowski said he estimated this year's grain output at 23.5 to 24 million tonnes, and that much of the grain may be of low quality.
